extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students in philosophy of mathematics, formal verification, and automated reasoning; mathematicians and computer scientists interested in proof assistants and the epistemology of proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and modeling what it is to 'understand' mathematical proofs and how that understanding can be supported or reproduced by formal verification systems (proof assistants). Emphasis on the behavioral/outward criteria for understanding, mechanistic/functional accounts, and strategies for automated proof search.

rubrics_metrics.name: verbal_and_written_communication_as_correlates_of_understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: If we view at least the outward signs of mathematical activity as essentially linguistic, it seems reasonable to take verbal and written communication as reliable correlates of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verbal/written ability (e.g., stating a theorem, answering a question appropriately, presenting a proof) as observable indicators of mathematical understanding; acknowledge contrived counterexamples but permit bracketing them when focusing a theory of mathematical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: scope_limitation_and_screening_of_extraneous_states
rubrics_metrics.description: Our theory need not account for the full range of human behaviors; we should be able to screen off extraneous beliefs and desires, and assume nothing about an agent’s intent beyond the intent to perform mathematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the domain of a theory of mathematical understanding to behaviors and contexts relevant to mathematical activity to avoid problems introduced by irrelevant mental states (e.g., fear, mistaken beliefs about explosives).

rubrics_metrics.name: outward_criteria_are_necessary_and_sufficient_for_meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: What gives our theoretical terms meaning is the role they play in explaining the desired or observed behaviors; 'An "inner process" stands in need of outward criteria' (Wittgenstein). While these outward criteria are necessary, they are also sufficient to give our terms meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor concepts of understanding in externally observable criteria; treat hypothesized inner mechanisms as models invoked to explain those outward signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: functionalist_approach_to_mathematical_understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe mathematical understanding in terms of abilities and their interactions (functional roles) — e.g., the ability to 'recognize' a structure, 'determine' subgroups, 'apply' a lemma, or 'recall' a fact — which serve as mechanisms explaining observable behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model understanding as a network of interacting capacities (some behavioral, some abstract) whose hypothesized roles explain how observed proof-reading and proof-generation activities occur; permit talk of mechanisms as explanatory hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: theory_should_support_pedagogy_and_software_development
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory of mathematical understanding should not only characterize outward signs of understanding, but also provide some hints as to how they can be encouraged and taught, and be of service to computer scientists trying to write software that exhibits competent mathematical behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories on pragmatic usefulness: do they give guidance for exposition, teaching, and for designing proof-assistant behaviors or heuristics?

rubrics_metrics.name: proof_scripts_must_supply_sufficient_instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: A user's interaction with a proof assistant can be seen as an attempt to provide the computer with enough information to see that there is a formal axiomatic proof of the purported theorem. Alternatively, the formal 'proof scripts' can be viewed as providing instructions as to how to find a formal axiomatic derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct/acceptable script must contain enough structure and hints so the assistant can construct a formal derivation; success (certification) is treated as the assistant 'understanding' the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: goal-driven_sequent_style_proof_development
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof development in systems like Coq, Isabelle, and HOL-light is goal-driven: stating a theorem announces the goal; each step reduces open goals (often represented as sequents A, B, C ⇒ D) to simpler goals using logical rules (e.g., 'and introduction' splits a goal into two subgoals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proof steps by their effect on goals; use sequent-style reasoning and tree closure (branch closed when conclusion matches a hypothesis) as bookkeeping for verification systems and as a model for human 'step justification'.

rubrics_metrics.name: understanding_an_inference_as_justifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: In this context, 'understanding' a step of a proof means being able to justify the corresponding inference (e.g., explaining that from A and B we have E corresponds to proving the sequent A, B ⇒ E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment of understanding focuses on whether the justification for the inference can be made explicit (to a human or a machine); texts often omit these details because they are 'clear' to competent readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: three_sources_of_combinatorial_explosion_in_proof_search
rubrics_metrics.description: Three factors drive intractability in proof search: (1) excessive case distinctions (disjunction splits), (2) term instantiation for existential/universal quantifiers (choice of witnesses or instances), and (3) the need to import appropriate background facts and theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing proof-search methods, explicitly account for these sources (e.g., understand exponential blowup from repeated case splitting; manage unbounded term choices via unification/Skolemization; heuristically select relevant background theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: heuristic_strategies_for_managing_search
rubrics_metrics.description: Three broad strategies for automated reasoning: backward-driven search (backchaining from goal using rules), forward-driven search (derive potentially useful facts in advance), and combining methods for tractable subdomains (e.g., Nelson–Oppen combination of local decision procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proof methods by how they mix backchaining and forward derivation, how they avoid case explosion, and whether they exploit specialized solvers for local theories; design heuristics to drive choice of facts/instantiations by context and goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: decision_procedures_have_limited_scope_and_efficiency_issues
rubrics_metrics.description: In restricted contexts decision procedures exist (e.g., Presburger arithmetic; Tarski's real-closed fields), but decidability is exceptional (Gödel) and full decision procedures are often inefficient or infeasible for practical inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decision procedures when applicable, but prefer specialized or heuristic methods for typical mathematical inferences; evaluate approaches by practical tractability as well as theoretical decidability.

rubrics_metrics.name: importance_of_structural_features_and_local_methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural features of the mathematics that we care about can make principled and effective reasoning possible (e.g., separating additive and multiplicative reasoning, using canonical normal forms or rewrite systems), allowing combination of local methods to handle more complex inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and exploit domain structure to reduce search complexity; judge methods by how well they leverage such structure rather than resort to ad hoc 'mucking around'.

rubrics_metrics.name: recognition_abstraction_and_instantiation_in_algebraic_reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic reasoning proceeds by (i) recognizing that a domain instantiates an abstract algebraic structure (e.g., a group), (ii) abstractly reasoning about that structure, and (iii) instantiating the abstract results back to the concrete domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs by how effectively they perform recognition and instantiation steps (e.g., discovering the relevant group structure, applying Lagrange's theorem), and prefer arguments that suppress irrelevant detail and highlight the structural core.

rubrics_metrics.name: context_as_collection_of_ready-to-hand_facts_and_procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal verification the notion of a 'context' denotes a collection of facts and procedures that are 'ready to hand' — i.e., immediately available for use in verifying inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or building proof developments, make explicit the context (lemmas, definitions, tactics) assumed to be available; the richer and better-organized the context, the easier it is to justify higher-level inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: relativize_theory_of_understanding_to_agent_type_but_seek_common_structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Different agents (humans vs machines) have different strengths (humans good at diagrammatic pattern recognition; machines good at exhaustive calculation), so theories of understanding should be relativized to the agent class while still aiming to identify common structural aspects that explain successful performance for both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess methods both in terms of agent-specific practices (pedagogy vs programming) and in terms of shared structural principles that can inform design of proof systems usable by both humans and machines.
